t.1.82.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That king of kings, having gone to heaven, dwelt in the abode of the gods, honored by the thirty gods, by the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and likewise the Vasus.
t.1.82.2: Moving from the world of the gods to the world of Brahmā, that self-controlled protector of the earth, a doer of meritorious deeds, dwelt there for a long time; so it is heard.
t.1.82.3: Once that best of kings, Yayāti, came to Śakra; there, at the end of their conversation, that lord of the earth was questioned by Śakra.
t.1.82.5: This entire realm between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is yours. You are king in the middle of the earth, and your brothers are lords of the outlying lands.
t.1.82.4: When that Pūru, having taken on your old age, O king, wandered the earth in your form, and you then handed the kingdom over to him, what was he told by you? Tell me the truth here.
t.1.82.6: The one free from anger is superior to the angry, and likewise the forbearing is superior to the unforbearing; humans are foremost among non-humans, and in the same way the learned is foremost among the unlearned.
t.1.82.7: When reviled, one should not revile in return; the very anger of the one who forbears burns up the reviler, and he wins the reviler's merit for himself.
t.1.82.9: A man who wounds others to the quick, who is harsh of speech and pierces people with the thorns of his words, one should know to be the most luckless of men, carrying Nirṛti, the goddess of ruin, bound fast to his mouth.
t.1.82.8: One should not wound others to the quick, nor speak cruelly, nor take what is highest from a base man. One should not utter that harsh, searing speech, leading to the worlds of the wicked, by which another is made to tremble.
t.1.82.10: One should be honored by the good before one's face, and likewise be protected by the good behind one's back; one of noble conduct should always bear patiently the abusive words of the wicked and adopt the conduct of the good.
t.1.82.11: Arrows of speech fly forth from the mouth, and one struck by them grieves night and day; those that fall upon another's vital spots, a wise man should not loose against others.
t.1.82.12: For there is no such means of winning hearts in the three worlds as friendliness toward all beings, generosity, and sweet speech.
t.1.82.13: Therefore gentle words should always be spoken, and harsh words should never be spoken at all. One should honor those worthy of honor, one should give, and one should never beg.
